raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old Indian male with HIV-positive status was admitted to our hospital with chief complaints of large-volume watery stools without blood or mucus, 3-4 times a day for 4 months with recent exacerbation for 1 week. This was also associated with nausea, loss of appetite, significant weight loss, generalized weakness, and dysphagia to solids. He denied personal or family history of allergies. He was diagnosed with HIV infection 17 years ago and was on treatment with antiretroviral drugs, namely raltegravir, lamivudine, and efavirenz. He was also diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 5 months back for which he was on treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. He unintentionally lost 20 kg of weight over the past 4 months. He further denied the use of laxatives or any complementary or alternative medications. He had stable vital signs, was cachectic, and had a normal systemic examination. His workup for chronic diarrhea included a normal thyroid function test and no opportunistic infections or helminthic infestation. Stool analysis including culture was negative for Clostridium difficile toxin, Cryptosporidium, Vibrio cholerae, acid-fast bacteria, or any other parasites. Serum IgE concentration was also within the normal range. Other investigations revealed hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL (13-18 g/dL), platelets 244,000/uL (140,000-440,000/uL), and total leukocyte count 4880/mm3 (4000-10000/mm3) with neutrophils 78.5% (40%-75%), lymphocytes 16.2% (20%-45%), and eosinophils 0.8% (1%-6%). His total protein was 5.4 g/dL (6.60-8.70 g/dL), albumin 1.8 g/dL (3.97-4.94 g/dL), absolute CD4 count 89.91/mm3 of blood (400-1600/mm3 of blood), absolute CD8 count 427.68/mm3 of blood (280-1400/mm3 of blood), CD4 (helper T-cells)% 11.1% (28-58%), CD8 (suppressor T-cells)% 52.8% (19-49%), CD4/CD8 0.21 (1.2-3.3), and HIV-1 viral load by TaqMan plasma (quantitative) 12,59,309 copies/mL.
On further investigations, esophagogastro duodenoscopy revealed white mucosal plaques in the esophagus consistent with esophageal candidiasis. The mucosa of the duodenum showed focal erosions with blunting of the villi as seen in Figure 1. Urease test was negative for Helicobacter pylori. Mucosal biopsies from the stomach and duodenum were taken. Histopathology study shown in Figure 2 revealed active inflammation in the gastric and duodenal mucosa with excess eosinophils (20 eosinophils/high-power field) and no microorganisms. This was consistent with EGE. He also had a colonoscopy which was normal. Rifampicin was stopped during this admission for a period of 2 weeks. However, the persistence of diarrhea ruled out drug-induced EGE. He was then started on oral prednisolone 40 mg once daily. The frequency of stools decreased and consistency improved. Prednisolone was gradually tapered over a period of 2 months. This was associated with an increase in the frequency of watery stools like before resulting in a readmission with dehydration and weight loss.
The patient was restarted on oral prednisolone 60 mg once daily. Along with cessation of diarrhea, his appetite and weight improved during follow-up after 30 days. On 6-month follow-up, he has regained 18 kg and has normal stools. He is currently on oral prednisolone 40 mg once daily.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old HIV-positive Indian male presenting with a 4-month history of chronic large-volume watery diarrhea (3-4 episodes daily, worsening over 1 week), 20 kg weight loss, and solid-food dysphagia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with 4 months of non-bloody, non-mucoid large-volume watery diarrhea that acutely worsened 1 week prior to admission, accompanied by nausea, anorexia, generalized weakness, dysphagia to solids, and a 20 kg unintentional weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV-1 infection 17 years prior (maintained on raltegravir, lamivudine, and efavirenz) and pulmonary tuberculosis 5 months prior (on isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic watery diarrhea, anorexia, 20 kg weight loss, weakness, nausea, and dysphagia to solids; denied laxative or herbal use and had no personal or family history of allergies.

objective.physical_examination: Cachectic appearance with stable vital signs and an unremarkable systemic physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL (13-18 g/dL), platelets 244,000/uL, and WBC 4,880/mm3 (neutrophils 78.5%, lymphocytes 16.2%, eosinophils 0.8%). Biochemistry showed hypoproteinemia (total protein 5.4 g/dL [6.60-8.70 g/dL]), severe hypoalbuminemia (albumin 1.8 g/dL [3.97-4.94 g/dL]), normal thyroid function, and normal serum IgE. Stool microscopy and cultures were negative for Vibrio cholerae, Clostridium difficile toxin, Cryptosporidium, AFB, and ova/parasites.
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological/virological workup showed CD4 count 89.91 cells/mm3 (11.1%), CD8 count 427.68 cells/mm3 (52.8%), CD4/CD8 ratio 0.21, and plasma HIV-1 viral load of 1,259,309 copies/mL. Colonoscopy was normal. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed esophageal candidiasis (white plaques) and duodenal mucosal erosions with villous blunting (rapid urease test negative for H. pylori). Gastric and duodenal mucosal biopsies demonstrated active mucosal inflammation with marked eosinophilic infiltration (20 eosinophils/HPF) and no microorganisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed primary eosinophilic gastroenteritis (EGE) and esophageal candidiasis in an advanced HIV/TB patient, established by gastroduodenal histopathology after ruling out Vibrio cholerae, opportunistic enteric pathogens, and rifampicin-induced enteropathy (via a 2-week rifampicin withdrawal trial).
Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral prednisolone 40 mg daily, resulting in rapid resolution of diarrhea; when symptoms relapsed upon steroid tapering at 2 months, oral prednisolone was restarted at 60 mg daily and tapered to 40 mg maintenance, achieving complete remission of diarrhea and an 18 kg weight gain at 6-month follow-up.
